title: CUL3-mediated NRF2 dysregulation in TP53-driven non-small cell lung cancer: neddylation-associated structural perturbations.
authors: Dharmalingam P, Sudandiradoss C
abstract: CUL3 encodes Cullin-3, the scaffold of Cullin-RING Ligase 3 (CRL3), which mediates proteasomal degradation of NRF2 through KEAP1-dependent ubiquitination. While canonical NRF2 alterations such as KEAP1 or NFE2L2 mutations are well characterised in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the role of CUL3 mutations remains poorly defined. We hypothesised that CUL3 missense variants are conditionally enriched in TP53-altered NSCLC, with the EGFR-oncogenic subset as a defined disease background rather than a synergistic requirement. A multi-cohort NSCLC dataset (n = 47,862; 10,228 with oncogenic EGFR mutations and confirmed CUL3 coverage) was interrogated using two-layer Fisher's exact testing and logistic regression with an EGFR × TP53 interaction term, and validated transcriptomically in TCGA LUAD/LUSC. CUL3 mutations showed conditional enrichment in the TP53-mutant EGFR background (OR = 2.92, p = 4.68 × 10-29); the non-significant EGFR × TP53 interaction (OR = 0.86, p = 0.547) confirmed that enrichment is driven by TP53 loss rather than EGFR synergy. CUL3-mutant tumours showed elevated NRF2 activation across three independent signatures, with increased proliferative signalling and altered drug metabolism. All-atom molecular dynamics simulations of wild-type, L321F, G402E and M711I CUL3:KEAP1 complexes in inactive and neddylation-active states revealed variant-specific conformational behaviour. L321F drove the neddylated complex into a conformationally restricted state with reduced backbone flexibility, decreased radius of gyration, and a shifted free energy minimum, whereas G402E showed progressive destabilisation and M711I remained comparable to wild-type. Free energy landscape analysis confirmed a shifted conformational energy minimum in L321F + NEDD8 relative to wild-type, indicating impaired catalytic flexibility despite intact complex formation. These findings define CUL3 as a TP53-associated modifier of NRF2 regulation within EGFR-driven NSCLC, operating through allosteric rigidification of the neddylation-active CRL3 complex.

title: Real-World Treatment Outcomes and Prognostic Factors in Metastatic EGFR-Mutated Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Single-Center Study from a High-Volume Tertiary Chest Hospital.
authors: Koçanoğlu A, Ünsal O, Kuş F et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a distinct molecular subgroup responsive to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). This study evaluated real-world treatment outcomes and prognostic factors in patients with EGFR-mutated metastatic NSCLC. Methods: This retrospective study included 124 patients treated with first-line EGFR-TKIs between January 2017 and 30 August 2025 at a tertiary center. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and prognostic factors were assessed using Cox proportional hazards models. Results: The median age was 66 years, and 63.7% of patients were female. The most common mutation was exon 19 deletion (65.3%). Median OS for the entire cohort was 31.7 months, and median PFS was 16.3 months. In multivariate analysis, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS), histopathological subtype, uncommon EGFR mutations, and bone metastasis were statistically significantly associated with OS in multivariable Cox regression analysis. Among patients receiving second-line treatment, median PFS was 16.7 months with osimertinib and 4.1 months with platinum-based chemotherapy; these nonrandomized treatment-specific outcomes were considered descriptive. Conclusions: In conclusion, the survival outcomes observed in our cohort were generally consistent with previously published real-world data in EGFR-mutant metastatic NSCLC. ECOG performance status and bone metastasis were significantly associated with OS, while associations involving histopathological subtype and uncommon EGFR mutations should be considered exploratory given the small subgroup sizes and limited statistical power. These findings provide real-world evidence on treatment patterns and survival outcomes among patients with EGFR-mutant metastatic NSCLC in Türkiye.

title: Comprehensive Analysis of Next-Generation Sequencing and ARMS-PCR for Detecting EGFR S768 Mutations in Chinese Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Patients.
authors: Kou B, Chen S, Zheng Q et al.
abstract: Background: Accurate detection of mutations at the EGFR S768 site is crucial for selecting appropriate treatment regimens for patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This study compared Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) and amplification refractory mutation system polymerase chain reaction (ARMS-PCR) for detecting EGFR S768 mutations in Chinese NSCLC patients. Methods: This study retrospectively analyzed 20,731 molecular pathology tests (8345 by NGS and 12,386 by ARMS-PCR). Results: The detection rate of EGFR S768 variants was significantly lower by ARMS-PCR than by NGS (0.40% vs. 1.15%, p < 0.001). The variants detected by ARMS-PCR were predominantly S768I, whereas NGS identified a broader spectrum, including S768I, S768_D770dup, S768_V769delinsIL, and S768_V769insLDS. Furthermore, the EGFR S768I mutation frequently co-occurred with other EGFR mutations, while insertion mutations at or near the EGFR S768 site rarely coexisted with other EGFR mutations (95.08% vs. 3.03%, p < 0.001). Notably, three cases with S768_V769delinsIL or V769_D770insSVV detected by NGS were identified as S768I by ARMS-PCR, which potentially affected the selection of patients' treatment plans. The sequence variations such as c.2307_2308insAGCGTGGTG, c.2303_2305delinsTCT, and c.2303_2305delinsTTT may be the reasons for the inconsistency between ARMS-PCR and NGS, due to possible non-specific primer binding. However, this remains a hypothesis based on sequence comparison and requires further experimental validation. Conclusions: Complex mutations or insertions around EGFR S768 site may cause discordant results between ARMS-PCR and NGS. NGS was recommended to confirm the EGFR S768 variants when the patient experiences rapid disease progression during treatment with EGFR S768I-directed targeted therapy.

title: Carpobrotus edulis Flower Extract Exerts Cytotoxic and Apoptotic Effects on A-549 Lung Cancer Cells: Phytochemical Profiling and In Silico EGFR Interaction Screening.
authors: Huwaimel B, Abouzied AS, Abd Rabo MM et al.
abstract: Medicinal plants serve as critical reservoirs of bioactive scaffolds for targeted cancer therapeutics. This study evaluated the antiproliferative potential of Carpobrotus edulis methanolic flower extract across a panel of human cancer cell lines, including pancreatic (Panc-1), breast (MCF-7), liver (HepG-2), and lung (A-549) malignancies. Screening assays revealed potent, dose-dependent cytotoxicity in an MTT-based viability assay, with A-549 lung cancer cells being the most sensitive of the four tested cancer cell lines (IC50 = 3.62 ± 0.34 μg/mL). Selectivity over non-malignant cells was not assessed. Flow cytometry showed an increase in the S-phase fraction and in Annexin V-positive cells, and ELISA showed higher Bax and p53 and lower Bcl-2 in extract-treated A-549 cells, consistent with apoptosis through the intrinsic pathway. The measured caspase-3 concentration was lower after treatment, and the assay does not distinguish pro-caspase-3 from cleaved caspase-3. Phytochemical profiling via GC-MS identified a diverse array of bioactive metabolites, predominantly triterpenoids, phytosterols, fatty acid derivatives, and cyclitols. To explore EGFR as a putative target, an in vitro EGFR kinase assay was combined with molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Among the profiled metabolites, the cyclitol derivative mome inositol displayed the most favorable docking score binding affinity toward the EGFR kinase domain (-7.35 kcal/mol), establishing robust hydrogen-bonding networks with key catalytic residues within the active site. Furthermore, a 100 ns MD simulation revealed the relative thermodynamic stability of the mome inositol-EGFR complex with more favorable RMSD, RMSF, hydrogen bond and radius of gyration profiles than the co-crystallized reference ligand. Collectively, these integrated in vitro, phytochemical, and in silico findings indicate that methanolic extract of C. edulis flowers exerts potent anticancer activity predominantly through mitochondrial-mediated apoptosis complemented by a computationally predicted interaction between its major cyclitol constituent and the EGFR kinase domain. These results establish the extract as a promising early-stage anticancer lead and provide a clear rationale for advancing to mechanistic studies, with in vivo validation reserved for subsequent investigations.

title: LLPS-Driven Membraneless Organelle Activity Landscape Reveals Molecular Subtypes, Immune States, and Prognostic Stratification in Lung Adenocarcinoma.
authors: Yan H, Yang N, Zhang L et al.
abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) drives the formation of membraneless organelles (MLOs) that regulate cellular compartmentalization and diverse biological processes. However, the landscape and clinical relevance of MLO-associated activity in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remain unclear. We integrated curated MLO-associated gene sets with transcriptomic data to estimate MLO activity using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis. MLO-related molecular subtypes were identified via consensus clustering, and an integrative machine learning framework was used to develop and validate the Membraneless Organelle Risk Score (MLORS) across independent cohorts. We further examined associations of MLORS with immune features, genomic alterations, and predicted treatment sensitivity and evaluated the function and phase-separation properties of E2F7 in vitro. MLO-associated activity was broadly dysregulated in LUAD, with high-MLO and low-MLO subtypes exhibiting distinct immune profiles and survival outcomes. High MLORS was associated with poorer survival, a computationally inferred immune-suppressed microenvironmental profile, higher tumor mutational burden, and lower predicted sensitivity to selected EGFR-targeted agents and chemotherapy. E2F7 formed nuclear condensates with LLPS-like properties and promoted lung cancer cell proliferation and migration in vitro. These findings link transcriptionally inferred MLO activity to the heterogeneity and prognosis of LUAD, support MLORS as a candidate prognostic stratification tool, and identify E2F7 phase-separation behavior as a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

title: Mechanism-Matched Pharmacology of Resistance in EGFR-Mutant NSCLC: Genomic Bypass, Lineage Plasticity, Antibody-Drug Conjugates, and Candidate Biophysical Targets.
authors: Seo Y
abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) often responds to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors but develops heterogeneous resistance. This structured narrative review integrates clinical and experimental evidence on resistance after osimertinib and intensified EGFR-directed therapy. It distinguishes on-target EGFR alterations, MET and ERBB-family bypass, downstream signaling, oncogenic fusions, histologic transformation, epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, and drug-tolerant persistence, linking each mechanism to an appropriate assay and treatment context. We evaluate next-generation EGFR inhibitors, EGFR-MET combinations, bispecific antibodies, platinum-pemetrexed intensification, and antibody-drug conjugates directed at HER3, TROP2, or HER2. Clinical validation is assessed separately from mechanistic causality, with attention to allelic phase, central nervous system exposure, target engagement, unbound drug concentration, predictive biomarkers, and safety. Ion channels and transporters, including ANO1/TMEM16A, LRRC8/VRAC, KCa3.1, hERG, STIM-ORAI, TRP, and pH regulators, remain exploratory candidate targets. Available evidence for their role in acquired osimertinib resistance is largely indirect; expression or general tumor biology does not establish disease-specific dependency. A mechanism-matched development pathway using paired tissue and plasma sampling, relevant resistant models, causal perturbation, and pharmacodynamic validation is proposed. Clinical decisions should follow validated mechanisms rather than extrapolated biophysical hypotheses.

title: Real-World Effectiveness and Safety of Tarlatamab in Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Systematic Review.
authors: Peshin S, Takrori E, Lal BM et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tarlatamab, a delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3)-targeted bispecific T-cell engager, has demonstrated clinical efficacy in previously treated small cell lung cancer (SCLC). However, its effectiveness and safety in routine clinical practice, particularly among patients underrepresented in clinical trials, remain incompletely characterized.
OBJECTIVE: To systematically review available real-world evidence regarding the effectiveness and safety of tarlatamab in patients with SCLC.
METHODS: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261345046). PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and ScienceDirect were searched for observational studies reporting real-world effectiveness or safety outcomes. Of 141 identified records, 134 remained after duplicate removal, and five retrospective studies met the eligibility criteria. Study characteristics, effectiveness outcomes, and adverse events were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity in patient populations, outcome definitions, and follow-up.
RESULTS: Five retrospective real-world studies were included. Reported partial or objective response proportions ranged from 35.2% to 66.7% across selected predominantly de novo SCLC cohorts, with estimates frequently restricted to response-evaluable subsets. The EGFR-mutant transformed SCLC cohort was analyzed separately. In one cohort, the reported objective response rate was 66.7% (20/30), corresponding to documented responses in 41.7% (20/48) of all treated patients. Median progression-free survival ranged from 1.7 to 4.9 months across reported analyses. Patients with EGFR-mutant transformed SCLC demonstrated less favorable outcomes, with partial response in 7.1% (1/14) of response-evaluable patients and median overall survival of 2.7 months. Cytokine release syndrome occurred in 54.2-72.7% of patients in selected cohorts, while ICANS occurred in 23.3-47.6%, with substantial variation across study populations and treatment protocols. The overall certainty of evidence was very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Available real-world evidence suggests that tarlatamab demonstrates clinically meaningful antitumor activity in previously treated SCLC, including patients with adverse baseline characteristics. However, effectiveness estimates are limited by small sample sizes, selection of response-evaluable populations, and heterogeneous outcome assessment. The relatively high incidence of ICANS reported in several real-world cohorts warrants particular attention, although differences in patient characteristics and toxicity ascertainment limit direct comparisons with clinical trials. Larger prospective studies are needed to establish real-world effectiveness and optimize toxicity management.
REGISTRATION: CRD420261345046.

title: Pulmonary Enteric Adenocarcinoma: From Diagnostic Attribution and Molecular Biology to Biomarker-Guided Clinical Pharmacology.
authors: Hung HY, Lee MH, Wu KL et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Pulmonary enteric adenocarcinoma (PEAC) is a rare lung tumor with intestinal differentiation and marked overlap with metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma. Misclassification can substantially alter therapeutic decisions. This review integrates contemporary diagnostic, molecular and treatment evidence with an emphasis on clinical pharmacology. Methods: In this narrative review, we critically appraised major classification documents, primary clinicopathologic studies, comparative genomic analyses, contemporary PEAC molecular cohorts, pooled outcome reports and landmark biomarker-defined non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) trials published through September 2026; supplementary pharmacology and trial-record verification was performed in October 2026. Results: Accurate attribution requires coordinated gastrointestinal evaluation, morphology and a panel of pulmonary and enteric markers; paired sequencing or methylation profiling may help in selected cases. KRAS and TP53 are recurrent alterations, while uncommon EGFR, ERBB2 and kinase-fusion events can inform biomarker-matched treatment. Reported immune features are heterogeneous, and mismatch-repair gene alterations should not be conflated with confirmed microsatellite instability. A pooled analysis of 127 patients (126 published) reported a median overall survival of 14 months in advanced/metastatic disease but did not establish comparative treatment efficacy. Drug interactions, CNS activity and treatment-related lung injury require attention; non-G12C RAS inhibitors remain unvalidated in PEAC. Conclusions: Stage IV management should follow molecularly appropriate NSCLC principles while carefully distinguishing directly observed PEAC evidence from extrapolated trial data. Multicenter registries and prospective molecularly annotated studies are urgently needed.

title: Real-World Eligibility for FLAURA, FLAURA2, and MARIPOSA in Patients with EGFR-Mutated Advanced NSCLC: A Retrospective Single-Center Study.
authors: Marchesi S, Ambrosini P, Cavalli C et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: First-line treatment options for EGFR-mutated NSCLC have expanded beyond osimertinib monotherapy following the FLAURA2 and MARIPOSA trials, which demonstrated improved long-term outcomes with combination strategies, albeit with increased toxicities. Given that randomized controlled trials (RCTs) typically enroll highly selected patients (pts), evaluating the representativeness of these cohorts in real-world (RW) practice is essential to inform RCT applicability.
METHODS: We retrospectively identified patients with EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC treated with first-line osimertinib at Fondazione IRCCS Istituto Nazionale dei Tumori, Milan, between January 2019 and August 2025. Clinical characteristics were collected, and eligibility for FLAURA, FLAURA2, and MARIPOSA was assessed according to the respective trial criteria. For survival analyses, patients were classified as trial-eligible or trial-ineligible according to FLAURA eligibility criteria, as all patients received first-line osimertinib.
RESULTS: Overall, 135 pts were included in the analysis; median age was 67 years (IQR 57-76), 17% had ECOG PS 2, and 11% harbored uncommon EGFR mutations. Only 31 patients (23%) met eligibility criteria for all three trials, whereas 91 (67%) were ineligible for all. The most frequent exclusion criteria included symptomatic CNS disease or spinal cord compression, ECOG PS 2, and EGFR mutation assessment by cytology or liquid biopsy. Both real-world progression free survival (rwPFS) and overall survival (OS) were numerically longer in trial-eligible than trial-ineligible patients (20.1 vs. 18.2 months and 29.9 vs. 22.3 months, respectively). Patients with negative prognostic characteristics such as ECOG PS ≥ 2, uncommon EGFR mutations, and liver metastases had significantly shorter OS, while other predefined risk factors showed only numerical trends.
CONCLUSIONS: A substantial proportion of patients treated with first-line osimertinib in routine practice would not have met the eligibility criteria of pivotal EGFR-mutated NSCLC trials. Trial-ineligible patients had numerically shorter survival, likely reflecting adverse baseline characteristics. These findings highlight the limitations of direct extrapolation of RCT results to real-world populations.

title: Precision Perioperative Treatment for Resectable Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: Current Status and Perspectives.
authors: Isaacs DJ, Park CJ, Zha L et al.
abstract: The treatment paradigm for resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) continues to evolve toward precision perioperative strategies. Despite curative-intent surgery, disease recurrence remains common. Adjuvant tyrosine kinase inhibitors have substantially improved disease-free survival and, in selected populations, overall survival, particularly for patients with sensitizing EGFR mutations or ALK rearrangements. Targeted therapies for other actionable genomic alterations (AGAs), including RET fusions, remain investigational. Adequate tissue acquisition and comprehensive molecular profiling before treatment initiation are therefore essential for optimal treatment selection. For patients without sensitizing EGFR mutations or ALK rearrangements, neoadjuvant or perioperative PD-(L)1 blockade combined with platinum-based chemotherapy has become a standard of care for eligible patients with resectable stage II-III NSCLC, improving pathological response, event-free survival, and, in select trials, overall survival. Multidisciplinary reassessment of resectability following neoadjuvant treatment is particularly important for borderline-resectable disease. Patients subsequently deemed unresectable require individualized management, potentially including definitive chemoradiotherapy followed by consolidation immunotherapy. Although cross-trial comparisons suggest advantages of neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy over adjuvant-only immunotherapy, direct randomized comparisons are lacking. The incremental benefit of postoperative immunotherapy after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy remains uncertain for selected patients. Future priorities include optimizing treatment sequencing, improving pathological complete response rates, refining radiographic and molecular response assessment, investigating resistance mechanisms, and integrating circulating tumor DNA-based minimal residual disease detection into individualized postoperative treatment. Whether surgery can be safely omitted in exceptional responders also warrants prospective investigation. Together, these advances support a biomarker-driven, response-adapted approach to precision perioperative NSCLC management.

title: The risk and economic burden of interstitial lung disease in patients with non-small cell lung cancer treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors and targeted therapies.
authors: Kwon S, Kim YH, Byun JY et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite improved survival with targeted therapies and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), evidence regarding the risk and economic burden of drug-induced interstitial lung disease (DI-ILD)-a potentially fatal adverse event-remains limited. We evaluated drug- and generation-specific risks of DI-ILD and its associated economic burden.
METHODS: Using the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service (HIRA) claims database (January 1, 2012-May 31, 2023), we identified patients treated with ICIs, epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors (EGFRis), or anaplastic lymphoma kinase inhibitors (ALKis). Incidence rates (IRs) and hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for ILD were estimated using stabilized generalized propensity scores weighting and Cox proportional hazards models. After 1:4 propensity score matching, healthcare costs and resource utilization during ILD treatment period were compared between patients with and without ILD.
RESULTS: Among 12,744 ICI users, 44,689 EGFR and 5,655 ALK prescription records, 111, 178, and 33 cases of ILD were identified, respectively. Compared with nivolumab, pembrolizumab (HR, 2.14; 95% CI, 1.12-4.11) and atezolizumab (HR, 1.80; 95% CI, 0.96-3.38) showed higher ILD risk. First- (HR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.44-1.00) and third-generation EGFRis (HR, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.22-0.89) had significantly lower risks than second-generation EGFRis. Compared with third-generation ALKis, first-generation (HR, 0.15; 95% CI, 0.03-0.70) and second-generation ALKis (HR, 0.20; 95% CI, 0.04-0.89) showed significantly lower risks of ILD. ILD was associated with higher healthcare costs and utilization, including hospitalization costs (2.11-5.24 times), infection and respiratory medication costs (2.72-13.88 times), hospitalization admissions (1.69-3.84 times), length of stay (1.66-2.57 times), and emergency room visits (1.21-5.58 times).
CONCLUSION: Given the substantial economic burden DI-ILD imposes, understanding differential risks of DI-ILD across treatment options could inform treatment selection and enable more timely management.

title: AI-based prediction of actionable genomic alterations from H&E-stained slides.
authors: Hwang W, Lopez-Rios F, Firozvi K et al.
abstract: Precision oncology based on the identification of actionable genomic alterations (AGAs) has been transformative in the care of solid tumors, yet optimal treatment selection is often hindered by tissue exhaustion and slow turnaround times. Artificial intelligence (AI) addresses these barriers by predicting AGAs directly from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained slides. Recent landmark studies, including the prospective EAGLE and ANNAR trials, have demonstrated that deep learning models can identify alterations such as EGFR in non-small cell lung cancer and FGFR in urothelial cancer across diverse global cohorts. By providing near-instant, non-destructive results, AI-based prediction can triage patients for molecular testing or clinical trials at the time of initial diagnosis. This perspective evaluates the maturing evidence base and outlines a pragmatic pathway for integrating these tools into clinical practice. Ultimately, these models offer the opportunity to extract critical molecular information from slides generated in every laboratory worldwide and to significantly improve timely access to the rapidly evolving therapeutic landscape of solid tumors.

title: Characteristics and outcomes of patients with advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer harboring a HER2-activating mutation: a real-world retrospective cohort study using a US clinico-genomic database.
authors: Le X, Chouaid C, Lopez-Rios F et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2/ERBB2) mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is associated with poor prognosis and limited treatment options.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used electronic health records from US academic and community cancer centers to describe characteristics and treatments of patients with HER2-mutated locally advanced/metastatic NSCLC initiating first-line (1 L) therapy between January 1, 2015, and March 31, 2024, in a real-world setting. Endpoints included real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS) and overall survival (OS) by line of therapy and in subgroups of interest.
RESULTS: Of 158 patients included (median age 69 years, 43.0% with Y772_A775dup [YVMA] mutation), 50.6% had ≥ 2 lines of therapy. Common 1 L therapies were chemotherapy + immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI; 36.1%) and chemotherapy (27.8%); common second-line (2 L) therapies were ICI (23.8%), chemotherapy + ICI (16.3%), and HER2-targeted antibody-drug conjugate (ADC; 16.3%). Median rwPFS/OS was 5.7/17.5, and 4.3/11.2 months, following initiation of 1 L and 2 L treatment, respectively. Median rwPFS ranged from 4.4 to 8.9 months and median OS from 15.7 to 16.0 months, following initiation of 1 L chemotherapy with or without ICI. Median rwPFS following initiation of 2 L treatment with ICI ± chemotherapy, chemotherapy ± monoclonal antibody, or HER2-targeted ADC ranged from 3.0 to 4.7 months, and OS from 10.8 to 23.4 months. Outcomes appeared to be descriptively inferior in patients with YVMA mutations versus other subgroups.
CONCLUSIONS: Overall outcomes were unsatisfactory, including in patients who had received chemotherapy ± ICI or HER2-targeted ADC in any line, highlighting the need for more effective targeted therapies.

title: TROP-2-Directed ADC Could Be New Standard for Some NSCLCs.
abstract: In the phase III Opti-TROP-Lung06 trial, patients with newly diagnosed PD-L1-negative, advanced nonsquamous non-small cell lung cancer without targetable alterations who received the TROP-2-directed antibody-drug conjugate sacituzumab tirumotecan and the PD-1 inhibitor pembrolizumab experienced a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 15 months. In comparison, those patients who received standard chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab experienced a median PFS of 5.7 months.

title: Intracranial Activity of Deruxtecan-Based Antibody-Drug Conjugates in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Brain Metastases: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Prospective Trial Cohorts.
authors: Tykocki T, Szalecki K
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Brain metastases are common in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have shown intracranial activity in trial subgroups, but intracranial data had rarely been pooled.
METHODS: MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, registries, and congress sources were searched through 21 September 2026 for prospective trials reporting central nervous system (CNS) outcomes of ADC monotherapy in NSCLC (PROSPERO CRD420261516140). Intracranial objective response rate (icORR) in measurable brain metastases was pooled with a random-intercept logistic model. Risk of bias and GRADE certainty were assessed.
RESULTS: Eight prospective cohorts (139 patients; six molecularly selected) of deruxtecan-based ADCs were included. Pooled icORR was 32% (95% CI, 25-41%; 45/139; I2 = 0%; prediction interval, 24-43%), and pooled intracranial disease control was 83% (69-92%; five cohorts). In TUXEDO-3, the only dedicated prospective CNS trial, restricted to active metastases, icORR was 30% (6/20). CNS progression-free survival hazard ratios versus chemotherapy were 0.48 (0.23-0.98) and 0.75 (0.53-1.06). Certainty was very low for single-arm response and low for comparative outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: Deruxtecan-based ADCs produced intracranial responses in one third of patients with measurable brain metastases from previously treated, predominantly oncogene-driven NSCLC, including active disease. Limited randomized data are compatible with delayed CNS progression. Prospective trials with CNS-specific endpoints are needed.

title: Therapeutic Strategies After Immunotherapy Failure in Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: Mechanisms of Resistance and Emerging Treatment Approaches.
authors: Kanayama M, Takenaka M, Uramoto H
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the treatment landscape of advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but disease progression during or after immunotherapy remains a major therapeutic challenge. ICI failure is biologically and clinically heterogeneous and may manifest as primary resistance, acquired resistance, oligoprogressive disease, hyperprogressive disease, or disease recurrence following treatment discontinuation. These distinct patterns may require different therapeutic approaches. In this review, we summarize the current evidence for treatment strategies after immunotherapy failure in advanced NSCLC. Cytotoxic chemotherapy remains a key subsequent-line treatment, though evidence supporting enhanced chemotherapy sensitivity after prior ICI exposure is largely derived from retrospective or non-randomized studies. Docetaxel plus ramucirumab is an established treatment option, but its specific efficacy after ICI failure has not been confirmed in randomized trials. Local therapies, including stereotactic body radiotherapy and salvage surgery, may provide meaningful local control in carefully selected patients with oligoprogressive or otherwise localized disease, though prospective evidence remains limited. ICI rechallenge generally has limited activity after progression during active ICI treatment, whereas re-exposure may be considered in selected patients after planned treatment completion or discontinuation because of immune-related adverse events. Biomarker development, including tissue biomarkers, circulating tumor DNA, circulating tumor cells, and emerging tumor-immune profiling approaches, may facilitate more individualized treatment selection. Overall, management after immunotherapy failure should be guided by the pattern and tempo of disease progression, prior treatment history, and the feasibility of systemic and local treatment. Further prospective studies are needed to establish effective treatment strategies and validated biomarkers for patient selection.

title: Risk prediction models for postoperative pneumonia in lung cancer patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Li C, Jiang Y, Wang Y
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative pneumonia (POP) is a common complication after lung cancer surgery. Numerous risk prediction models for POP have been developed. However, the quality and predictive performance of these models remain unclear.
METHODS: A literature search was carried out in CNKI, Wanfang Database, VIP Database, SinoMed, PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and Web of Science. The search covered studies on risk prediction models for postoperative pneumonia in lung cancer patients from inception to July 20, 2026. The research question was formulated using the PICOTS framework. Data extraction was performed following the Critical Appraisal and Data Extraction for Systematic Reviews of Prediction Modelling Studies (CHARMS), and risk of bias and applicability were assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST). Meta-analysis was conducted using STATA 17.0 software.
RESULTS: A total of 26 prediction models from 20 studies were included. Models were developed predominantly with logistic regression, with machine-learning approaches used in two studies. Common predictors included age, operation time, smoking, diabetes mellitus, preoperative pulmonary function, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and TNM stage. All studies exhibited a high risk of bias, mainly due to inadequate data sources and suboptimal reporting in the analysis domain; 16 studies also raised applicability concerns, mainly due to participant selection limited to specific lung cancer subgroups. The pooled AUC from the meta-analysis was 0.89 (95% CI: 0.87-0.91).
CONCLUSION: Although existing postoperative pneumonia prediction models for lung cancer patients show good discriminative performance, their clinical applicability is limited by a high risk of bias, which may lead to overestimation of discrimination. Future studies should develop more robust models with larger sample, rigorous designs, and multicenter external validation.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier CRD42024554224.

title: Transcutaneous Electrical Acupoint Stimulation Combined with General Anesthesia in Minimally Invasive Surgery for Lung Cancer: A Randomized, Patient- and Assessor-Blinded, Sham-Controlled Trial.
authors: Zhang Y, Yan W, Wei J et al.
abstract: Background: We aimed to clarify (1) the analgesic efficacy of transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation (TEAS) combined with general anesthesia during minimally invasive lung cancer surgery and (2) exploratory neural network correlates of acupuncture-drug combined anesthesia. Methods: Eligible patients receiving general anesthesia for minimally invasive lung cancer surgery were randomly allocated to perioperative TEAS or sham-TEAS in this randomized, patient- and assessor-blinded, sham-controlled trial. Postoperative patient-controlled intravenous analgesia (PCIA) was administered. Outcome measures included postoperative visual analog scale (VAS) pain scores, sufentanil consumption via PCIA, and total/effective PCIA pump presses. Perioperative electroencephalography (EEG) was acquired using a 22-lead recorder, and brainwave power spectra were analyzed using Fourier transform. Repeated-measures analysis of variance (RM-ANOVA) was applied to serial postoperative VAS scores at 6, 24 and 48 h. Independent-samples t-tests compared cumulative sufentanil consumption at 6, 24 and 48 h postoperatively. Post hoc simple-effect comparisons were performed as exploratory analyses without multiplicity adjustment. The EEG sub-study was exploratory; false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction was used to control multiple comparisons across electrodes and frequency bands. Results: In total, 109 patients were randomized. A significant group-by-time interaction was detected for postoperative VAS scores (F(1.599,171.124) = 68.287, p < 0.001). Simple-effect analyses revealed lower VAS scores in the TEAS group at postoperative 6 h (mean difference -1.900, 95%CI -2.181 to -1.619, p < 0.001) and 24 h (mean difference -1.391, 95%CI -1.645 to -1.138, p < 0.001), with no between-group difference at 48 h (mean difference -0.066, 95%CI -0.320 to 0.187, p = 0.605). The TEAS group also exhibited reduced PCIA sufentanil consumption at 6, 24 and 48 h postoperatively, alongside fewer total and effective PCIA pump presses. After FDR correction, exploratory EEG analysis identified potential dipole-related power differences in the prefrontal, occipital, parietal (postcentral gyrus), temporal and diencephalic regions, predominantly within beta-band oscillations (14-35 Hz). Conclusions: These exploratory findings suggest that TEAS combined with general anesthesia may reduce postoperative pain and analgesic requirement. This potential benefit may arise from TEAS-mediated modulation of pain-related neural networks; however, the observed intraoperative EEG oscillatory differences are exploratory neurophysiological correlates and do not confirm causal mechanisms.

title: Omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids in Cancer Cachexia and Inflammation: Mechanisms and Delivery Innovations.
authors: Cintoni M, Leonardi E, Meo E et al.
abstract: Cancer-associated cachexia and chronic systemic inflammation remain among the most challenging complications in oncology, impairing prognosis, treatment tolerability, and survival. This narrative review examines the mechanistic rationale and clinical evidence for omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), principally eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), as adjunctive nutritional and metabolic support agents in this setting, drawing on randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and mechanistic studies, alongside the oral, enteral, parenteral, and nanotechnology-based platforms used to deliver these fatty acids. In experimental models, predominantly cancer cell lines and tumor-bearing rodents, EPA and DHA act on multiple oncological processes, including suppression of pro-inflammatory cytokine synthesis, remodeling of the tumor microenvironment, inhibition of tumor cell proliferation, induction of apoptosis, and attenuation of skeletal muscle catabolism via the ubiquitin-proteasome system and the IGF-1/PI3K/Akt/mTOR axis; in patients, the most consistent mechanistic correlate is a reduction in circulating inflammatory biomarkers. Bioavailability varies substantially by molecular form, with re-esterified triglycerides outperforming ethyl esters and emerging micellar and phospholipid nanoformulations achieving markedly higher absorption in pharmacokinetic and preclinical studies. In advanced non-small cell lung cancer with established cachexia, a meta-analysis of small randomized trials suggests that at least 2 g EPA+DHA per day for six weeks or more may yield modest gains in body weight and quality-of-life scores; this signal, however, derives mainly from pooled analyses and has not been consistently reproduced in individual trials, including large negative trials in mixed cancer populations. Across broader oncological populations, reduction in inflammatory biomarkers is the most consistent finding, effects on chemotherapy tolerability are suggestive but of low certainty, and effects on lean mass and overall survival remain inconclusive. Consistent with ESPEN and ESMO guidance, omega-3 PUFAs should be regarded as metabolic and nutritional support within multimodal cachexia care, not as an anticancer treatment. Omega-3 PUFAs are a biologically grounded and potentially useful, but not yet clinically established, intervention in oncological nutrition, but adequately powered trials with harmonized endpoints, standardized formulations, and stratification by cancer type and cachexia stage are still needed to translate this mechanistic signal into definitive therapeutic protocols.

title: Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Narrative Review.
authors: Datta D, ZuWallack R
abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by airflow limitation from the narrowing of small airways and damage to lung parenchyma, resulting in exercise intolerance. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) provides a comprehensive assessment of exercise capacity and of the integrated responses of the respiratory, cardiovascular, muscular and metabolic systems. It helps clinicians understand the mechanisms of dyspnea, informs treatment decisions and can evaluate the effectiveness of pulmonary rehabilitation and other treatments. CPET can also detect coexisting conditions, such as heart failure, myopathy or deconditioning, that worsen exercise intolerance in COPD despite treatment. Recognizing these comorbidities allows them to be investigated and treated in their own right. Because CPET is resource-intensive, it is best used selectively, as a phenotyping and problem-solving tool, and it is important that pulmonologists know when to request it and how to interpret it. In this review, the mechanisms of exercise limitation in COPD and the physiological measurements obtained during CPET are described, and the CPET patterns that distinguish ventilatory limitation from cardiac, pulmonary vascular and other causes of exercise intolerance are compared. Testing protocols, the interpretation of results in relation to bronchodilator therapy, and safety and contraindications are summarized. Developments since previous reviews and guidelines on COPD and lung cancer fitness, as well as recent evidence on ventilatory efficiency and prognosis are highlighted, with emphasis on integrative interpretation. Clinical applications are illustrated with an algorithm and a case example, and limitations, cost, barriers to implementation and future research are discussed.

title: Pulmonary Large-Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma: Molecular Heterogeneity, Current Treatment and the Emerging Precision-Oncology Paradigm.
authors: Lee TH, Ma JY, Hung HY et al.
abstract: Pulmonary large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) is a rare, aggressive malignancy with substantial biological heterogeneity. Genomic studies identify SCLC-like and NSCLC-like spectra, but genomic categories overlap incompletely with transcriptional states. Morphology remains essential: neither neuroendocrine marker positivity nor RB1 status alone distinguishes LCNEC from small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). This narrative review integrates diagnostic limitations, stage-based management, and the clinical implications of profiling. Surgery with systematic nodal assessment is central for resectable disease; postoperative platinum chemotherapy has greater support than perioperative immunotherapy. In advanced disease, platinum-etoposide is a commonly used reference regimen. Retrospective associations involving platinum-gemcitabine or platinum-taxanes in RB1-wild-type tumors remain hypothesis-generating and should not be extended to pemetrexed. LANCE, a durvalumab phase II trial, and preliminary NEJ044 findings provide prospective chemo-immunotherapy observations, although randomized LCNEC-specific evidence remains absent. No standard second-line regimen is established. Rare actionable drivers may support matched treatment, whereas DLL3-directed approaches and FGL1/SPINK1-associated strategies require clinical validation. We propose an evidence-qualified framework separating stage-based care, individualized molecular considerations, and clinical-trial strategies.

title: Antibody-Drug Conjugates Plus Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors for Sustained Disease Control in Advanced Solid Tumors.
authors: Xu M, Yin J, Li Y et al.
abstract: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) improve outcomes in selected advanced solid tumors, but clinical benefit does not establish pharmacological synergy. This narrative review evaluates disease control during ADC-ICI therapy and the implications for radiotherapy in recurrent or metastatic disease. Prolonged disease control is assessed primarily through progression-free survival in randomized trials; response duration provides complementary evidence among responders. Overall survival, quality of life, and toxicity determine the broader clinical value of treatment. Randomized trials support specific regimens in urothelial, breast, and lung cancers, whereas negative studies argue against generalization across drugs and diseases. Antigen expression, payload delivery, and the immune microenvironment may contribute to heterogeneous outcomes, but their clinical roles remain incompletely established. Reported treatment durations do not define optimal stopping times. Radiotherapy can address local symptoms, but whether it improves systemic disease control during ADC-ICI therapy remains unproven. We distinguish direct three-modality evidence from indirect ADC-radiotherapy and ICI-radiotherapy studies and identify priorities for patient selection, outcome assessment, and safety monitoring. Current evidence supports regimen-specific treatment selection and toxicity-directed modification, not routine radiotherapy addition or elective drug withdrawal across disease settings.

title: The Role of Surgery in Small-Cell Lung Cancer in the Chemoimmunotherapy Era.
authors: Petrella F, Cara A, Cassina EM et al.
abstract: The modern role of surgery in small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) is best understood as an unresolved question rather than a settled recommendation. Older randomized trials established that surgery has no role in unselected SCLC, but these trials predate PET-CT staging, endosonographic mediastinal staging, and immunotherapy, and therefore cannot answer today's clinical question in modern, invasively staged, node-negative disease. Current guideline support for resection in cT1-2N0 SCLC rests largely on retrospective, registry-based data (SEER, NCDB) that carry substantial selection bias rather than randomized confirmation. Meanwhile, the nonsurgical comparator has advanced: chemo-radiotherapy plus durvalumab consolidation, validated in the ADRIATIC trial, now defines the modern limited-stage standard against which any surgical strategy must be benchmarked. Molecular subtyping (ASCL1, NEUROD1, POU2F3, inflamed phenotypes; TP53/RB1 co-alteration) and emerging neoadjuvant and perioperative chemo-immunotherapy data introduce plausible, though unproven, avenues for patient selection and treatment sequencing. Surgical tissue also offers a translational platform for studying immune microenvironment, clonal evolution, and treatment resistance. This review argues that surgery for SCLC is neither obsolete nor an established standard in isolation. Its future role requires two distinct lines of prospective investigation: comparisons of upfront surgery with neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy followed by resection, which address treatment sequencing, and comparisons of surgery-based multimodality treatment with definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy followed by durvalumab, which address the incremental value of surgery over contemporary nonsurgical care.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Thoracic Surgical Oncology: Technical Foundations and Applications in Lung and Esophageal Cancer Surgery.
authors: Cassidy R, Razzaq S, Howell A et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated in lung and esophageal cancer surgery, where treatment decisions require integrating imaging, clinical risk, and operative findings. This narrative review describes the technical foundations of surgical AI and examines its applications in thoracic surgical oncology, with particular emphasis on robotic surgery and the evidence supporting clinical use.
METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE was searched for English-language publications addressing AI, machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and robotic thoracic surgery. Targeted searches and examination of reference lists identified additional studies. Publications were selected for clinical and technical relevance, prioritizing original investigations, external or prospective validation studies, and reporting guidelines. Applications were examined across preoperative assessment, intraoperative assistance, and postoperative care.
RESULTS: Preoperative applications include pulmonary nodule characterization, prediction of nodal disease and invasive tumor features, anatomical reconstruction, and assessment of response to neoadjuvant therapy. Intraoperative systems have demonstrated anatomical segmentation, surgical-phase recognition, and augmented reality guidance. Other models address technical performance, postoperative complications, recurrence, and survival. Selected studies report improved predictive performance or earlier recognition of critical structures; however, much of the evidence remains retrospective and institution-specific. External validation is limited, and evidence that AI assistance reduces complications or improves oncologic outcomes remains insufficient.
CONCLUSIONS: AI offers tools for interpreting information relevant to thoracic cancer surgery, but technical accuracy alone does not establish clinical benefit. Prospective, multicenter evaluations should determine whether AI changes consequential surgical decisions and improves patient outcomes. Reliable performance under difficult operative conditions, integration into clinical workflow, and surgeon oversight remain essential to adoption.

title: Development of OnkoMoveNurse: a nurse-led physical activity support programme for people with lung cancer in oncology day clinics - a modified delphi consensus study.
authors: Engst R, Tanner CY, Wiskemann J et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Physical activity (PA) is a key factor in reducing treatment side effects and improving well-being in patients with lung cancer. However, PA levels during systemic antitumor therapy remain low. Nurses, who play a central role in oncology day clinic care, are well positioned to support patients in becoming physically active during cancer treatment. This project aimed to develop an evidence-based prototype of a nurse-led PA support programme for people with lung cancer in the oncology day clinic.
METHOD: A consensus panel of 15 members participated in a three-round modified Delphi consensus process (10/22-04/23). The process combined focus group discussions for the development of the programme, an anonymous online voting round to establish consensus on PA exercises identified through a scoping review, and a final consensus meeting to refine and confirm the programme.
RESULTS: The panel concluded that a list of exercises alone was insufficient to support sustainable PA promotion. This consensus process resulted in the development of OnkoMoveNurse, a nurse-led PA programme prototype comprising three core components: a PA toolkit, a safety protocol, and a communication guide. These components are underpinned by two overarching principles: interprofessional teamwork and person-centred care.
CONCLUSIONS: OnkoMoveNurse represents a prototype of a nurse-led PA programme designed to facilitate PA promotion within routine oncology day clinic care. While nurses coordinate the intervention, its implementation relies on collaboration across the interprofessional team. Future implementation studies are required to evaluate the safety, feasibility, and potential effects of OnkoMoveNurse and to explore its adaptation to other oncology populations.

title: Low-dose CT Screening and Smoking Cessation: Separate and Joint Associations with Mortality among Ever-Smokers Eligible for Lung Cancer Screening.
authors: Wang H, Frick C, Sha S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Smoking cessation intervention is increasingly recognized as a core component of high-quality lung cancer screening (LCS). However, real-world evidence that compares the health effects of low-dose CT (LDCT) screening, smoking cessation, and their combination among screening-eligible current smokers remains limited.
METHODS: We conducted a post-hoc analysis of data of the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST), defining recent quitting as smoking cessation within 2 years before enrolment as a proxy for cessation occurring close to screening initiation. Cox proportional hazards models were used to quantify associations of screening allocation and smoking cessation with LC-specific and all-cause mortality.
RESULTS: Among 31,560 continuous smokers and recent quitters included in the analysis, 7,197 (22.8%) died from any cause during a median follow-up of 12.3 years. Of 30,915 participants included in cause-specific analyses, 1,783 (5.8%) died from LC. Among current smokers eligible for LCS, LDCT was associated with 12% lower LC mortality than chest radiography (CXR) (HR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.79-0.97), but no significant reduction of all-cause mortality (HR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.93-1.03). In the CXR arm, recent quitting was associated with substantially lower LC and all-cause mortality than continued smoking (HRs, 0.62 and 0.68; 95% CIs, 0.51-0.76 and 0.62-0.75, respectively), with similar reductions observed among recent quitters in the LDCT arm.
CONCLUSIONS: For screening-eligible current smokers, recent quitting was associated with substantially larger reductions in LC and all-cause mortality than those associated with LDCT screening. These findings reinforce the importance of integrating effective smoking cessation interventions into LCS programs.

title: Exploratory Integrated Clinical Score and ICF-Defined Functioning in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Cross-Sectional Study.
authors: X Pencea X TG, Bălteanu MA, Roșu SM et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Spirometry is essential for respiratory assessment but does not fully characterize disability or everyday functioning. This study examined whether an exploratory Integrated Clinical Score (ICS), combining spirometric impairment and systemic inflammation, was associated with selected International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) categories in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) entering pulmonary rehabilitation. Methods: This cross-sectional baseline analysis included 62 consecutively recruited adults with histologically confirmed NSCLC. The ICS combined standardized FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC, and natural-log-transformed neutrophil-to-lymphocyte and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratios; higher values indicated greater disease burden. Eleven prespecified ICF categories were rated; eight categories formed the primary analysis set, while three Environmental Factors categories were analysed separately as exploratory. Associations were examined using Spearman correlations with Benjamini-Hochberg correction and proportional-odds models adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and smoking status. Results: Higher ICS values were associated with greater difficulty in energy and drive functions, exercise tolerance, walking, daily routine, housework, and recreation and leisure (ρ = 0.34-0.39; all adjusted p < 0.05). Emotional functions were not associated with the ICS; pain reached significance only in the adjusted model (OR 1.61, 95% CI 1.02-2.55). Separate component analyses indicated that these associations were predominantly driven by the lung-function subscore, whereas the inflammation subscore was not significantly associated with any primary ICF category after correction for multiple testing. A 1-SD increase in the ICS was associated with a 0.37-point increase in the summary functional-difficulty index (95% CI 0.13-0.61; p = 0.003). Conclusions: The exploratory ICS was associated with functioning across several ICF domains, but these associations were predominantly driven by its lung-function component, and incremental value from adding inflammatory markers was not demonstrated. The ICS should therefore be regarded as a hypothesis-generating research construct rather than a validated clinical instrument; further studies should assess its reproducibility and incremental value beyond lung function alone.

title: Trousseau Syndrome Manifesting as Recurrent Embolic Stroke in ROS1-Positive Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer: A Case Report.
authors: Wu TT, Cheng SL
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Trousseau syndrome is a paraneoplastic hypercoagulable state manifesting as recurrent thromboembolism. Lung adenocarcinomas harboring specific driver mutations, such as ROS1 rearrangements, are associated with a significantly increased risk of these events and related complications.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 61-year-old non-smoking female with stage IV ROS1-positive lung adenocarcinoma developed bilateral cerebral and cerebellar infarctions. While aspirin therapy was initiated, she still experienced a recurrent ischemic stroke involving the left middle cerebral artery, leading to a diagnosis of Trousseau syndrome. However, the course was further complicated by pneumonia and respiratory failure. Anticoagulation with apixaban was initiated. A third embolic event subsequently occurred, involving a right middle cerebral artery occlusion with associated subarachnoid hemorrhage and hemorrhagic transformation. Despite intensive management, the patient's condition deteriorated, and she passed away.
CONCLUSIONS: Trousseau syndrome significantly impairs the prognosis of lung cancer patients, especially with specific driven genes, such as ROS-1 gene re-arrangement. This case highlights the deteriorating prognosis of cancer-associated thrombosis, which can be refractory and requires heightened clinical vigilance.

title: An integrative systems biology framework decodes peripheral blood transcriptomic signatures, systemic interactome networks, and candidate targets in lung squamous cell carcinoma.
authors: Farzadifar E, Sorouri S, Zarrini M et al.
abstract:
AIM: To characterize systemic transcriptomic signatures and identify candidate hub genes associated with lung squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC) in peripheral blood using an integrative systems-biology approach.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Peripheral blood transcriptomic data from GSE252168 (32 LSCC and 32 controls) were analyzed using GEO2R/limma. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were subjected to protein-protein interaction, functional enrichment, network-hub, transcription-factor motif, and exploratory DrugBank analyses. Fifteen prespecified hub genes were evaluated in an independent whole-blood cohort (GSE198048) and compared with primary tumor tissue from TCGA-LUSC (511 tumors, 51 normal samples).
RESULTS: GSE252168 yielded 3,689 DEGs (|log2FC| > 0.2, adjusted p < 0.05), with enrichment of ribosomal/translation, proteostasis, and metabolic processes. KLF12, KLF16, and KLF9 were identified as putative upstream regulators. Five hub genes (RPL10A, RPL22, RPS4X, RPS27A, and RPS14) showed targeted external replication within the prespecified 15-gene panel, all being downregulated. In TCGA-LUSC, 10/15 hub genes were differentially expressed, while only 5/15 showed directional concordance with blood.
CONCLUSION: Peripheral blood transcriptomics reveals systemic molecular alterations in LSCC, with candidate hub genes and pathways requiring independent and experimental validation.

title: How could MAGE-A4 targeting transform synovial sarcoma care?
authors: Hatipoglu E, Napolitano A, Pozas J et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Synovial sarcoma is a rare and aggressive type of soft tissue sarcoma with poor clinical outcomes for patients with locally advanced or metastatic disease. The main treatment for advanced disease is chemotherapy.
AREAS COVERED: Recent developments in adoptive cell therapies had a transformative effect on synovial sarcoma treatment. A new novel target for synovial sarcoma treatment is melanoma-associated antigen A4 (MAGEA4) which is a cancer-testis antigen that is highly expressed in tumor with limited expression in normal tissue. The accelerated regulatory approval of the engineered T-cell receptor (TCR) therapy targeting MAGEA4 (afamitresgene autoleucel) is the first TCR therapy approved for solid tumors and is a milestone in synovial sarcoma treatment. We discuss the scientific rationale for MAGEA4 therapy & review the evidence supporting its use as well as challenges such as access & the manufacturing process.
EXPERT OPINION: The approval of MAGE-A4-targeted TCR is a milestone in treatment of synovial sarcoma. For the first time, a precision immunotherapy has demonstrated efficacy and durable clinical responses. This achievement fundamentally challenges the long-held assumption that engineered cellular therapies have limited success in treatment of solid tumors.

title: Immunotargeting of Cervical Cancer Cells with the Adaptor CAR T-Cell Platform RevCAR.
authors: Jones-Cifuentes N, Arndt C, Loureiro LR et al.
abstract: The Prostate Stem Cell Antigen (PSCA) is not only overexpressed in prostate cancer (PC) but also in many other tumors, including cervical cancer (CC). The adaptor chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) platform RevCAR can be used for immunotargeting of PSCA-expressing tumor cells. We found that the CC cell line SiHa natively expresses PSCA. The expression was sufficient for redirection of RevCAR T-cells using recently described RevCAR target modules (RevTMs) directed against PSCA. Like almost all PC cell lines, however, SiHa cells also downregulate their PSCA expression in cell culture. To overcome this limitation, we established artificially PSCA-overexpressing SiHa cells. Retargeting of RevCAR T-cells strictly depends on PSCA-directed RevTMs and PSCA-expressing target cells. It leads to (i) upregulation of CD69, Perforin and Granzyme B, (ii) lysis of target cells with EC50 values in the picomolar range, and (iii) cytokine secretion of IFN-γ, TNF-α, GM-CSF and IL-2. Phenotypic analysis shows a prominent increase in memory RevCAR T-cells but only a slight increase in exhausted cells, indicating a low level of tonic signaling of RevCAR T-cells. Together, our data supports an efficient and safe immunotargeting of PSCA-expressing CC cells with the RevCAR technology.

title: Microenvironmental IL13 Rα2 Expression and Enable Extracellular Vesicle-Mediated Antigen Transfer in Glioblastoma.
authors: Wang Y, Urak R, Chen C et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Interleukin-13 receptor alpha 2 (IL13Rα2), expressed in more than 75% of glioblastomas (GBM), is a promising chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell target. We investigated how microenvironmental stresses regulate IL13Rα2 expression and whether extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated antigen transfer modulates CAR T cell killing. Methods: Patient-derived brain tumor and other GBM cell lines were exposed to hypoxia, desferrioxamine (DFO), or reduced fetal bovine serum (FBS). Western blotting assessed IL13Rα2 expression and recovery following reoxygenation. Fluorescence imaging evaluated EV interactions with recipient cells, and cytotoxicity assays assessed CAR T cell killing. Results: Hypoxia and DFO markedly suppressed IL13Rα2 expression. Exposure to 1% oxygen for 48 h reduced protein levels by 40-70%; expression recovered to near-baseline levels within 48 h of reoxygenation. Reduced FBS concentrations for 48 h also decreased IL13Rα2 expression compared with 10% FBS. Findings suggested potential contributions from ubiquitin-dependent degradation and transcriptional mechanisms. IL13Rα2-expressing EVs showed a slight increase under hypoxia. Fluorescence imaging confirmed that IL13Rα2-containing EVs attached to or entered recipient GBM cells within hours. EV-mediated antigen transfer increased CAR T cell killing by 3-5%. Conclusions: Hypoxia and nutrient availability dynamically regulate IL13Rα2 expression, while EVs can transfer the antigen between GBM cells and modestly enhance CAR T cell killing. These findings highlight reversible antigen modulation and EV-mediated antigen redistribution as mechanisms that could inform strategies to overcome antigen escape and improve immune targeting in GBM.

title: Dynamic SPECT imaging kinetic modelling characterises tracer influx and efflux in tumour-infiltrating CAR T cells.
authors: Bugallo-Blanco E, Taprogge J, Murray I et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T cell therapies for solid tumours face challenges regarding inefficient trafficking to the tumour site, limited extravasation and impaired persistence within an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Non-invasive imaging approaches capable of capturing the dynamic behaviour and biodistribution of CAR T cells are therefore needed to better understand these barriers. This study explores the use of compartmental modelling to interpret technetium-99 m pertechnetate ([99mTc]TcO4-) uptake by CAR T cells co-expressing the sodium iodide symporter (NIS) reporter gene in a prostate cancer NSG mouse model using single-photon emission computed tomography computerised tomography (SPECT/CT).
RESULTS: Co-expression of hNIS with a prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) targeting CAR did not impair CAR T cell function and enabled non-invasive visualisation of CAR-hNIS T cell infiltration in vivo. Dynamic SPECT/CT imaging revealed clear differences in tumour uptake between CAR-hNIS treated mice and control groups. Compartmental modelling using a reversible two-compartment framework demonstrated increased tracer influx and reduced tracer efflux in CAR-hNIS treated tumours. These kinetic changes indicate that tumour signal arises from NIS-mediated tracer uptake and delayed tracer washout in tumours containing infiltrating CAR T cells, rather than from passive perfusion or non-specific delivery alone. Immunohistochemistry confirmed CAR T cell infiltration in the tumours.
CONCLUSIONS: This work establishes a proof-of-concept for applying kinetic modelling to interpret CAR T cell infiltration in vivo using dynamic hNIS-based SPECT imaging. By distinguishing tracer delivery from tracer washout kinetics and correcting for variability in tracer bioavailability, this approach provides a more sophisticated biological interpretation of tumour uptake than static imaging alone. These findings highlight the potential of integrating kinetic modelling into future quantitative cell-tracking strategies to improve the evaluation and optimisation of CAR T cell therapies for solid tumours.

title: Rewiring dendritic cell function with CLEC9A and DEC205 CARs.
authors: Niu C, Dai X, Gao H et al.
abstract: Dendritic cells (DCs) are central orchestrators of antitumor immunity, yet their therapeutic potential is constrained by dysfunction and inadequate activation within solid tumors. Here we report chimeric antigen receptor-engineered DCs (CAR-DCs) that prime T cells and reprogram the tumor microenvironment. We identify the intracellular domains of CLEC9A or LY75 (DEC205) as essential for functional CAR-DC activity, enabling enhanced antigen uptake and cross-presentation and driving T cell expansion and function. CARs incorporating the CLEC9A or DEC205 intracellular domains triggered SYK phosphorylation and downstream signaling. In both conventional and humanized mouse models, CAR-DC therapy suppressed tumor growth and promoted expansion of tumor-reactive T cells. These findings establish CAR-DCs as scalable and clinically translatable platforms for next-generation solid tumor immunotherapy.

title: Secondary cancer after CAR-T cell therapy: A French pharmacovigilance analysis.
authors: Bassinet-Kiladjian L, Grandvuillemin A, Fresse A et al.
abstract:
AIMS: Cases of secondary cancers (SC) associated with Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T cell therapy have been reported in the literature prompting safety alerts from both the Food and Drug Administration and the European Medicines Agency after reports of T-cell lymphomas. Establishing causality between CAR-T therapy and SC in patients previously heavily treated for a hematological malignancy is challenging. To clarify this risk, we evaluated SC cases reported to Regional Pharmacovigilance Centers in France for patients with hematological malignancy treated with one of the six authorized CAR-T therapies.
METHODS: A query in the French Pharmacovigilance Database conducted on 01/24/2025 identified 20 SC cases with a suspected CAR-T specialty, representing 19 patients.
RESULTS: Most patients were male (63%), with a mean age of 65.2±6 years. Of these, 79% had received CAR-T treatment for B-cell lymphoma and 21% for myeloma. Only 3 of the currently available CAR-T therapies were reported as suspected drugs: tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel and idecabtagene vicleucel. The mean interval between CAR-T administration and SC diagnosis was 11 months (median of 9.5 months). Of the 20 SC, 11 were secondary hemopathies (6 acute myeloid leukemias, 4 myelodysplasias, and one cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with CAR-T cells detected in the blood and skin). The remaining 9 cases were secondary solid tumors including 3 skin neoplasms, 2 colon adenocarcinomas, one breast cancer, one relapse of oral squamous cell cancer, one jejunal leiomyosarcoma, one manubrial bone sarcoma (the latter two in the same patient). Most patients had established risk factors for these cancers, making CAR-T causality difficult to assess, except for the cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
CONCLUSION: Continuous long-term monitoring is essential to further evaluate the benefit-risk profile of CAR-T therapies, especially in settings with poor prognosis.

title: Restoring Activation-Linked Clusterin Loss Attenuates Tumor-Directed T Cell Dysfunction Associated with Reduced Translation and Proteostatic Stress.
authors: Segner C, Höbart J, Xue B et al.
abstract: T cell therapies with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells or T cell receptor (TCR) transgenic (tg) T cells are a promising approach in the treatment of solid malignancies but are limited by T cell exhaustion caused by chronic antigen stimulation. Clusterin (CLU) is a stress-associated molecular chaperone with cytoprotective functions in normal and malignant cells, but its role in therapeutic T cells is unclear. Here, we found that CLU expression is reduced in exhausted tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and decreases after prolonged stimulation of Ewing sarcoma (EwS)-directed TCR-transgenic T cells and GD2 CAR-T cells. To test whether reconstituting CLU affects T cell fitness, we engineered CHM1/HLA-A*02:01-directed ChoTCR-T cells and GD2 CAR-T cells to overexpress CLU. In ChoTCR-T cells, CLU overexpression reduced exhaustion- and apoptosis-associated features after repetitive tumor stimulation while preserving cytotoxicity. CLU-engineered ChoTCR-T cells showed improved infiltration of EwS spheroids, and moderately improved antitumor activity in a metastatic EwS model. Supportive experiments in a GD2/Nalm6 chronic-stimulation model indicated preserved CAR-T cell function after repetitive antigen exposure. Mechanistically, proteomics together with direct measurements of global translation and stress-response activation support a model in which CLU reduces proteostasis-linked translational stress during chronic stimulation. These findings identify CLU overexpression as a promising strategy to attenuate chronic-stimulation-associated dysfunction in tumor-directed T cells, as shown in two therapeutic T cell models of cancer in the young.

title: Endogenous Retrovirus-Targeted Immunotherapy for Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Supported by Cellular HERV-K Expression, Dependency and Efficacy of ERV Therapy in a Murine Model.
authors: Perez-Penco M, Scott TE, Engdal ES et al.
abstract: Human endogenous retrovirus-K (HERV-K/HML-2) has been associated with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but its functional relevance and the potential for HERV-directed immunotherapy remains unresolved. Here, we characterized HERV-K expression across 207 advanced NSCLC patient biopsies by total RNA-seq observing widespread expression of HERV-K Gag and Env antigen encoding sequences. The Env-ORF that disrupted HERV-K102 was strongly associated with interferon and antigen-presenting programs, identifying it as a marker of an immune-activated tumor state. shRNA-mediated knockdown of HERV-K in five NSCLC cell lines with distinct driver mutations impaired proliferation and survival. In separate experiments, exposure of these cell lines to treatment-related stressors, including cytokines (TNF-α and IFN-γ) and chemotherapy, revealed dynamic patterns of HERV-K protein accumulation with antigen expression retained, and in some cases increased. Immunotherapeutic targeting was performed using the ASB-XIV mouse NSCLC cell line and a murine ERV surrogate antigen using adenovirus to express murine leukemia virus (MLV) antigen on a mouse β-retroviral particle structurally related to HERV-K. This immunization was able to elicit significant protection against tumor challenge and additive benefit with anti-PD-L1 in therapeutic treatment, establishing proof-of-concept for ERV-targeted immunotherapy in a murine surrogate system rather than direct evidence of HERV-K-targeted efficacy. Our findings suggest an important role of HERV-K in NSCLC immunobiology and that adaptive immunity targeting HERV-K should be explored in the treatment of NSCLC patients.

title: Real-World Treatment Patterns and Sequencing of ALK-Inhibitors in ALK-Positive NSCLC Treated with Palliative Intent.
authors: Ay L, Krainer-Jacobs J, Lang-Stöberl A et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: ALK-rearranged non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a molecularly defined subtype that is highly sensitive to ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors (ALK inhibitors). With multiple generations of ALK inhibitors available, real-world data on treatment patterns and sequencing in routine clinical practice remain limited.
METHODS: This retrospective multicenter registry analysis included patients with ALK-positive NSCLC treated with palliative intent and enrolled in the LALUCA registry between November 2020 and September 2025 at four lung cancer centers in Vienna. ALK alterations were confirmed by next-generation sequencing. Demographic, clinical, and treatment-related data were analyzed descriptively.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight patients were included (median age, 54 years [range, 26-84]; 46.4% female). Most patients had stage IV disease (85.7%) and adenocarcinoma histology (92.9%). Overall, 49 systemic treatment lines were administered, including 41 ALK inhibitor treatment lines (22 second-generation and 19 third-generation). At data cut-off, 39.0% of ALK inhibitor treatment lines were ongoing, with a higher proportion of ongoing treatment observed among third-generation compared with second-generation ALK inhibitors (52.6% vs. 27.3%). The Kaplan-Meier-estimated median treatment duration was 287 days (95% CI, 172-NE) for second-generation and 736 days (95% CI, 376-NE) for third-generation ALK inhibitors. Objective response rates were 77.3% and 73.7%, respectively. Adverse events of any grade occurred in 73.2% of treatment lines, while grade ≥ 3 adverse events occurred in 12.2%. Dose reductions and temporary treatment interruptions were used to manage toxicity and allowed for treatment continuation in most affected treatment lines.
CONCLUSIONS: This multicenter real-world analysis provides insights into contemporary ALK inhibitor treatment patterns and sequencing in routine clinical practice. Third-generation ALK inhibitors were associated with longer observed treatment durations in this cohort, although these findings should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample size, retrospective analysis, and potential differences in treatment selection and follow-up. Overall, toxicity was generally manageable, with dose modifications and temporary treatment interruptions frequently allowing for continuation of ALK inhibitor therapy.

title: 68Ga-DOTATOC PET/CT Uptake and Physiological Impairment in DIPNECH: An Exploratory Case Series.
authors: Palamidas A, Tzilas V, Bouros D
abstract: Background/Objectives: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH) can cause respiratory symptoms and physiological impairment. We explored whether quantitative somatostatin-receptor imaging by positron emission tomography/computed tomography with gallium-68-labelled DOTATOC (68Ga-DOTATOC PET/CT) is associated with pulmonary physiology and nodule count in histologically confirmed DIPNECH. Methods: This retrospective, single-centre, hypothesis-generating series included six consecutive adults diagnosed during 2020-2025. Spearman correlations with exact permutation p-values and 95% confidence intervals related the maximum standardised uptake value (SUVmax) of the most avid lesion to diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO), forced expiratory flow between 25% and 75% of forced vital capacity (FEF25-75) and the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 s to forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC); index-lesion diameter and expected partial-volume recovery were examined. Analyses were exploratory and unadjusted for multiple comparisons. Results: All patients were women. SUVmax correlated inversely with DLCO (ρ = -0.90; p = 0.028) and FEF25-75 (ρ = -0.84; p = 0.044); the nodule-count-DLCO association was uncertain (ρ = -0.37; p = 0.50). Index lesions measured 3.6-4.7 mm, below the resolution of the PET system; lesion diameter was unrelated to SUVmax (ρ = -0.20), and the association with DLCO persisted after crude recovery correction (ρ = -0.66). Conclusions: Higher 68Ga-DOTATOC uptake of the most avid lesion accompanied greater physiological impairment in this six-patient series, and the differences in uptake were not explained by lesion size. Given the sample size, wide confidence intervals, multiple unadjusted comparisons, unadjusted comorbidities and sub-resolution lesions, these findings are hypothesis-generating only; they do not establish SUVmax as a marker of disease severity, an actionable threshold or a guide to biopsy, but support prospective investigation of somatostatin-receptor imaging in DIPNECH.

title: Association Between Hospital Size and Outcomes of ES-SCLC Treated with Chemo-ICI: A Real-World Database Study in Japan.
authors: Yamanaka Y, Iwasaki K, Uenishi T et al.
abstract: Background: Chemotherapy combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors is the standard first-line treatment for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. We evaluated whether hospital size, as a surrogate for institutional healthcare resources, was associated with treatment outcomes. Methods: This retrospective observational study used a nationwide electronic medical records database in Japan. Patients with extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC) receiving first-line platinum-etoposide plus atezolizumab or durvalumab between 2019 and 2022 were included. Patients were classified by hospital size (<500 vs. ≥500 beds) and compared after propensity score matching. The primary endpoint was time to treatment failure (TTF), and secondary endpoints included grade ≥ 3 hematological toxicities and hepatic impairments.
